period_summary: Citations cluster heavily in the 2nd–3rd centuries in anti-Jewish apologetic and passion theology, then continue in 4th–5th century christological debates. This concentration reflects the verse's central role in demonstrating Jesus as the suffering servant who interceded for transgressors.

citations.cited_text: He was numbered among the transgressors, and he bore the sins of many, and for their sins he was delivered up
citations.text_form_note: The phrase 'he was delivered up' (paredothē) closely follows LXX's παρεδόθη, while MT has 'he made intercession' (yaphgia). Justin's citation reflects the LXX tradition that emphasizes Christ's passion.
citations.theological_use: Justin employs this text to prove to Trypho that the Messiah's suffering and death for sinners was foretold in Scripture, countering Jewish objections that a suffering Messiah was incompatible with messianic prophecy.
citations.transmission_implication: Justin's citation attests an early Greek text form closely aligned with the LXX tradition circulating in Rome by the mid-2nd century.

citations.cited_text: He was numbered with the transgressors, and he bore the sins of many, and was delivered up on account of their sins
citations.text_form_note: Irenaeus follows the LXX reading 'was delivered up' (paredothē) rather than MT's 'made intercession.' The Greek textual tradition is clearly dominant in his citation practice.
citations.theological_use: Irenaeus uses this passage to demonstrate the unity of Old and New Testament revelation, showing that Christ's vicarious suffering was prophesied and that he fulfilled the role of the suffering servant by bearing humanity's sins.
citations.transmission_implication: The citation confirms LXX dominance in Greek-speaking Western churches by the late 2nd century, transmitted through liturgical and catechetical use.

citations.cited_text: He was reputed with the wicked and bore the sins of many and was delivered for their offences
citations.text_form_note: Tertullian's Latin reflects the Old Latin tradition based on the LXX, using 'traditus est' (was delivered) corresponding to Greek paredothē, not the MT's intercessory language.
citations.theological_use: Tertullian argues against Marcion's rejection of the Old Testament by showing that Christ's passion was foretold in prophetic Scripture, thus demonstrating continuity between the testaments and the same God in both.
citations.transmission_implication: This citation shows the LXX textual tradition had been translated into Old Latin by the late 2nd century in North Africa.

citations.cited_text: He was numbered among the lawless and bore the sins of many
citations.text_form_note: Clement uses 'anomōn' (lawless) for transgressors, consistent with LXX terminology. The citation omits the final clause but what is present aligns with the Greek tradition.
citations.theological_use: Clement employs the passage pedagogically to illustrate Christ as the divine teacher who descended to humanity's level, bearing sins to educate and redeem his pupils through salvific suffering.
citations.transmission_implication: The LXX text form was the authoritative scriptural witness in the Alexandrian catechetical school by the early 3rd century.

citations.cited_text: He was numbered with the transgressors
citations.text_form_note: Origen cites the opening phrase using LXX vocabulary. Though the citation is partial, his hexaplaric work shows awareness of textual variants, yet he consistently uses the LXX form in theological exposition.
citations.theological_use: Origen uses this text typologically to explain Jesus' crucifixion between two thieves as fulfillment of Isaiah's prophecy, demonstrating the spiritual correspondence between prophetic word and gospel event.
citations.transmission_implication: Despite Origen's knowledge of Hebrew and multiple text forms through his Hexapla, the LXX remained his primary citation text for Christian theological discourse.

citations.cited_text: He was numbered among the lawless, and he bore the sins of many, and because of their sins he was delivered up
citations.text_form_note: Eusebius provides a fuller citation closely matching the LXX, including the distinctive 'paredothē' (was delivered up) rather than any reference to intercession found in MT.
citations.theological_use: Eusebius marshals this prophecy as apologetic proof that Jesus' crucifixion with criminals and his bearing of sins was divinely foreordained, countering objections that crucifixion disproved messianic claims.
citations.transmission_implication: The LXX text form remained dominant in Palestinian Christianity in the early 4th century despite geographical proximity to Hebrew-speaking Jewish communities.

citations.cited_text: He was numbered among the lawless, and he bore the sins of many, and on account of their sins he was delivered up
citations.text_form_note: Cyril's direct commentary on Isaiah preserves the LXX reading with precision, using 'paredothē' and showing no awareness or preference for the MT's intercessory reading.
citations.theological_use: Cyril develops a sophisticated christological interpretation: Christ's being numbered with lawless ones demonstrates his voluntary kenosis and identification with sinful humanity, while his bearing sins accomplishes redemption through vicarious sacrifice.
citations.transmission_implication: By the 5th century, the LXX text form was so entrenched in Alexandrian exegetical tradition that even scholarly commentary shows no textual alternatives.

citations.cited_text: He was counted among the wicked and bore the sins of many and prayed for the transgressors
citations.text_form_note: Jerome uniquely among the fathers provides the MT reading 'prayed/interceded for transgressors' (oravit pro transgressoribus) based on Hebrew yaphgia, explicitly noting the difference from the LXX's 'was delivered up.'
citations.theological_use: Jerome emphasizes Christ's active priestly intercession for sinners, using the Hebrew text to highlight Jesus' ongoing mediatorial role, not merely passive suffering but active prayer for humanity's redemption.
citations.transmission_implication: Jerome's Vulgate translation from Hebrew represents a deliberate scholarly correction of the Old Latin tradition, introducing the MT text form into Latin Christianity for the first time.

transmission_synthesis: The patristic citation history reveals overwhelming dominance of the LXX text form across all regions (Rome, Alexandria, Caesarea, Carthage, Gaul) from the 2nd through early 5th centuries. Seven of eight fathers cite the distinctive LXX reading 'was delivered up' (paredothē) rather than the MT's 'made intercession' (yaphgia), indicating that the Greek translation became the Christian scriptural standard independent of the Hebrew. Only Jerome, working directly from Hebrew in the late 4th century, introduces the MT reading into Latin Christianity through his Vulgate revision. This pattern strongly supports the thesis that the LXX became 'Christian Scripture' (per Hengel) with its own transmission history separate from Jewish textual traditions, and that until Jerome's scholarly intervention, knowledge of divergent Hebrew readings had minimal impact on the text form circulating in Christian communities.
transmission_synthesis_plain: Early Christian writers from the 2nd to 5th centuries almost universally used a Greek translation that differs significantly from the Hebrew text at a key point: where Hebrew says the servant 'interceded' for sinners, the Greek says he 'was delivered up.' Only Jerome, translating directly from Hebrew around 400 CE, brought the Hebrew reading into Christian use. This shows Christians preserved and transmitted their own Greek scriptural tradition independently of Jewish communities.

notable_variants.reading: was delivered up (paredothē) for their sins
notable_variants.significance: This LXX reading emphasizes Christ's passive suffering and being 'handed over' to death, which became theologically central to patristic passion theology. It differs sharply from MT's active intercessory role, showing how translation shaped Christian soteriology and suggesting the LXX translator may have read a different Vorlage or interpreted the verse christologically avant la lettre.

notable_variants.reading: prayed/interceded for the transgressors (oravit/interpellavit pro transgressoribus)
notable_variants.significance: Jerome's citation from Hebrew (yaphgia') introduces the MT reading emphasizing Christ's active priestly intercession. This variant demonstrates that the Hebrew textual tradition preserved a theologically distinct portrait of the servant's agency that was unknown to Greek Christianity until the late 4th century, raising critical questions about which reading is original.

bibcrit_assessment.title: LXX Monopoly Until Jerome's Hebrew Intervention
bibcrit_assessment.reasoning: The most striking finding is the absolute uniformity of the LXX text form across diverse regions and three centuries, with no father prior to Jerome showing awareness of the significantly different Hebrew reading. This indicates that Christian scriptural transmission operated in complete independence from contemporary Jewish textual scholarship, and that theological interpretation was built on a Greek translation whose divergence from Hebrew at this crucial soteriological verse went unrecognized. Jerome's introduction of the MT reading represents not a return to an 'original' known to early Christianity, but the importation of an alien textual tradition that would eventually compete with but never fully displace the entrenched LXX form.
bibcrit_assessment.plain: For over 300 years, every Christian writer quoted this verse in a form saying Christ 'was delivered up,' not knowing the Hebrew said he 'interceded.' This shows Christians had their own textual tradition completely separate from Jewish scribes, and it raises the critical question: which reading goes back to the original prophet?

_validation.confidence_note: The overall thesis (LXX dominance until Jerome) is sound and well-established, but several specific citation references are imprecise or potentially misattributed.

flagged_claims.claim: Justin Martyr, Dialogue with Trypho, ch. 13
flagged_claims.reason: Dialogue ch. 13 cites Isaiah 52:10–54:6 extensively but the specific wording attributed here should be verified; Justin cites Isa 53 most fully in chs. 13 and 89, and the exact phrasing given may conflate sections.
Irenaeus cites Isa 53 in multiple places (e.g., AH 4.33.2, Epideixis 68); the specific reference to 4.33.11 with this exact wording needs verification.

flagged_claims.claim: Origen, Commentary on Matthew, Book 12, section on Mt 27:38
flagged_claims.reason: Book 12 of Origen's Commentary on Matthew covers Matt 16–17, not Matt 27. Commentary on the crucifixion narrative would fall in later books or the Commentariorum Series. This citation reference appears incorrect.

flagged_claims.claim: Clement of Alexandria, Paedagogus, Book 1, ch. 8
flagged_claims.reason: Paed. 1.8 discusses God's goodness and discipline; whether Isa 53:12 is cited there with this wording requires verification, as Clement's Isaiah citations are scattered.
DE Book 10 deals with the passion; Isa 53 is treated more fully in DE 3.2 and 10.8. The exact chapter reference needs verification.

flagged_claims.claim: the LXX translator may have read a different Vorlage
flagged_claims.reason: Stated speculatively but appropriately; however, the contrast between paredothē and yaphgia is more often explained as interpretive translation of the same consonantal text, not necessarily a different Vorlage.
Jerome resided in Bethlehem from 386 onward, not Jerusalem; minor but factually imprecise.

flagged_claims.claim: Eusebius's region listed as 'Caesarea' and Origen's as 'Caesarea'
flagged_claims.reason: Origen's Commentary on Matthew was composed in Caesarea, which is acceptable, but earlier works are Alexandrian; the regional attribution is oversimplified.

safe_claims: The MT reads yaphgia (interceded) while LXX reads paredothē (was delivered up) at Isaiah 53:12.
Jerome's Vulgate translates from Hebrew and renders the intercession reading.
Early Christian writers predominantly used the LXX text form of Isaiah 53.
The LXX 'was delivered up' reading aligned with NT passion theology (cf. Rom 4:25).
Jerome explicitly noted differences between Hebrew and LXX in his Isaiah commentary.
